summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743 was approved by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, promulgated on 24 May 2012, and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree banning gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for minors, modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to adolescents, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prison. Legal experts called the decree illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for adolescents' rights, and petitioned for judicial intervention.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people has risen sharply. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity in 2025, a record year averaging one every 38 hours, which the observatory described as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina. Trans activists in Buenos Aires, including figures from organisations named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, said in April 2025 that the Milei government's policies have made the community more vulnerable to violence, describing the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The gender-motivated-crime aggravating circumstance is currently not applied in practice. Argentina's Supreme Court left standing in April 2025 the life sentence for Gabriel Marino, convicted of the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravator that a cassation court had removed in 2020.

Argentina was the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws. Outright International's overview, updated in March 2026, nonetheless records negatives on same-sex relations, gender recognition and organisation registration, indicating deterioration in its current assessment.
tangentialFactors:
The gap between Argentina's statutory framework and its enforcement record is wide. The 2012 Gender Identity Law remains formally in force and was lauded internationally, but the February 2025 decrees narrowed its application to minors, and the Supreme Court's April 2025 refusal to reinstate the travesticidio aggravator means gender-motivated killings are not charged with the hate-crime enhancement that the statute contemplates.

Activist testimony from Buenos Aires in April 2025 links the deterioration in safety directly to the Milei government's policy direction rather than to general crime conditions, describing a chaotic and desperate situation for the trans community specifically.

The record 227 hate crimes logged in 2025 coincides with the year the decrees took effect, though the sources do not establish causation between the two.
localsOnly:
Legal gender change without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval remains available to Argentine residents under Law 26.743, subject to the February 2025 decree's restrictions on minors.

Marriage equality has been in force since 2010, and anti-discrimination protection is provided through a combination of national and provincial laws.

Transgender people in prison are subject to a separate decree governing their housing, issued February 2025, which legal experts have challenged as unconstitutional.

Organisations working on trans rights, including those named for Diana Sacayán and Lohana Berkins, continue to operate and to document violence, though Outright International's March 2026 assessment records a negative on organisation registration.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the February 2025 decrees have been struck down or modified by the courts since the legal challenges were filed is unresolved in the sources; the inventory records the challenge but no outcome.

The scope of the travesticidio aggravator's removal is unresolved: the sources state a cassation court removed it in 2020 and the Supreme Court declined to reinstate it in the Sacayán case in 2025, but whether the aggravator is unavailable in all cases or only on these facts is not sourced.

The Outright International overview's negative rating on organisation registration is recorded without a stated basis in the inventory, so the underlying restriction is not sourced here.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including passport marker conventions, are not covered by any source in this inventory.
